<reason>Both sides built coherent causal stories, but CON's rebuttal work was sharper and more damaging. The pivotal moment was CON's answer to PRO's own pressure question (B4.1): distinguishing the population of "victims/witnesses at the station" from "individuals already booked and flagged in jail." This directly attacked the load-bearing spillover mechanism PRO relied on throughout — that detainer compliance teaches victims not to call police — by showing these are legally and practically separate populations. PRO's closing tried to reconnect them by asserting that communities "blur" these categories, but this was a late, thin reassertion rather than a developed mechanism, leaving CON's distinction largely standing. CON also pressed effectively on the "illusory warrant power" question, forcing PRO to list ICE alternatives (administrative warrants, own-authority arrests) that CON plausibly characterized as rarely executable once someone is released on schedule. PRO's framing (one-day hold vs. a standing rule protecting dozens of future victims) was rhetorically strong and kept the moral stakes vivid, and PRO's federalism reframe ("declining to subsidize federal enforcement, not nullification") was a solid counter that CON never fully dismantled. But on the decisive comparative question — whose causal story survives scrutiny — CON's tighter, more surgical rebuttals and cleaner closing ("a name and a file" vs. "a theory about rumor") gave it the more resolved case. The debate was close and both sides argued with discipline, but CON's execution in the rebuttal rounds was the difference-maker.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's B4.1 answer to PRO's Q1 (Turn 8), distinguishing victims/witnesses from already-flagged jail arrestees, which undercut PRO's core spillover mechanism and was never fully repaired in PRO's closing.</best_rebuttal>
